sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Inspection evaluates (i) conformance of components to material specifications, (ii) conformance of construction methods to execution specifications, (iii) site or soil conditions needing changes to installation or design, (iv) short-term performance (load testing) and (v) long-term monitoring if contracted. Short-term monitoring (wall deflection, ground movement, nail load tests) is by the Owner or Contractor; long-term monitoring is usually by the Owner. The inspector keeps installation logs, a daily log and a field book.
sections.body: 9.1 Introduction (pp. 231-232). The chapter covers the most common aspects of soil nail wall inspection and monitoring, whatever the contracting approach and whoever is assigned inspection; additional measures may be needed for a given project. Inspection evaluates: (i) conformance of system components to material specifications; (ii) conformance of construction methods to execution specifications, if any; (iii) identification of site or soil conditions that require adjustment to the installation procedures or to the original design; (iv) conformance to short-term performance specifications (load testing); and (v) long-term monitoring, if required by contract. A valuable source is the Soil Nailing Field Inspector's Manual (Porterfield et al. 1994). Short-term monitoring is usually limited to measurements during and possibly shortly after construction and may include vertical and lateral wall deflection, ground movement near the wall and load testing of soil nails; long-term monitoring is less typical and usually continues the short-term measurements. Short-term monitoring can be by the Owner or the Contractor depending on the contracting approach; long-term monitoring is usually by the Owner. The inspection personnel ensure all required construction activities and testing are completed per the contract; the inspector must understand soil nail wall construction, be intimately familiar with the design drawings and specifications, carry the necessary safety gear and instruments (checking any Contractor-provided gear works), and keep soil nail installation logs, a daily log and field book.
key_points: Inspection: material conformance, method conformance, changed site or soil conditions, load testing, long-term monitoring
Applies whatever the contracting approach and whoever performs inspection
Reference: Soil Nailing Field Inspector's Manual (Porterfield et al. 1994)
Short-term monitoring: wall deflection, nearby ground movement, nail load tests; by Owner or Contractor
Long-term monitoring less typical, usually by the Owner
Inspector keeps soil nail installation logs, a daily log and a field book
sections.applicability: Scope and responsibilities of soil nail wall construction inspection and monitoring.

sections.title: Inspection of Construction Materials
sections.summary: Materials are controlled by visual examination, manufacturer or supplier certification, and laboratory testing of samples. Steel components are accepted on mill certifications; cement on producer certification pending grout compressive tests. Potable water needs no testing. Cement is stored dry and elevated; tendons on supports. Damaged corrosion protection is repaired or the tendon replaced; encapsulated tendons are tapped for voids (voids: replace); epoxy-coated tendons with bare steel or out-of-range coating are replaced.
sections.body: 9.2.1 Materials Inspection (p. 232): quality is controlled by visual examination for defects (poor workmanship, contamination, handling damage), certification by the manufacturer or supplier, and laboratory testing of representative samples. Steel components (tendons, bearing plates, nuts, washers, WWM, reinforcing bars) are normally accepted on mill certifications; cement on certification by the producer pending unconfined compressive testing on grout and observation of nail installation; centralizers, coatings, grout additives, sheathing, geocomposite drainage material and piping on manufacturer certificates; visual inspection for transport or storage damage is still necessary. Water for grout or shotcrete must be free of harmful chemical or organic material; potable water is generally suitable without testing. 9.2.2 Storage (pp. 232-233): materials kept in a suitable location and protected; cement (bagged or bulk) kept dry and elevated, bags not stacked too high (over-compaction); tendons on supports clear of the ground and moisture, spaced to prevent excessive bending that could compromise tolerances or minimum cover; other steel and drainage materials in suitable containers. 9.2.3 Inspection of Corrosion Protection (p. 233): corrosion protection of all tendons inspected on site before acceptance; damaged protection repaired if possible or the tendon replaced. Encapsulated tendons arrive assembled, with the sheath annulus grouted at the plant: inspect the encapsulation for cracks or scores (repairs per manufacturer procedures, subject to Owner approval); check a representative number for voids by lightly tapping with a steel rod; tendons with voids should generally be replaced, not repaired. Epoxy-coated tendons: avoid impact, dragging, excessive bending, field cutting; nicks and dents may be repaired with the manufacturer's kit, but tendons with bare steel or coating thickness outside the Chapter 7 range should be replaced. Galvanized tendons: inspect similarly, support well during lifting; repairs of limited damage strictly per the manufacturer.
key_points: Quality control: visual examination, manufacturer or supplier certification, laboratory testing
Steel components on mill certifications; cement on certification pending grout compressive tests
Potable water generally suitable for grout or shotcrete without testing
Cement dry, elevated, bags not stacked too high; tendons on supports spaced to prevent bending
Corrosion protection inspected on site before acceptance; damaged: repair if possible or replace
Encapsulated tendons: check for cracks or scores; tap with a steel rod for voids; voids: replace
Epoxy-coated: nicks repaired with manufacturer's kit; bare steel or out-of-range thickness: replace
sections.applicability: Acceptance, storage and corrosion-protection inspection of soil nail materials.

sections.title: Inspection of Construction Activities
sections.summary: Inspection is by qualified individuals: the Geotechnical Engineer, wall Designer or Specialty Contractor, a third party, or a combination; where a third party is not qualified for specialized tasks, the geotechnical engineer or wall designer completes them. In mass excavation the inspector checks it does not encroach on the partly built wall; bench excavation is to neat line and grade within tolerance. The inspector records face materials and moisture, unexpected soft zones, seepage or fill, raveling, face protection, and checks stability at least twice a day.
sections.body: 9.3.1 Introduction (pp. 233-234): inspection by qualified individuals; may be entirely by the Geotechnical Engineer, by the wall Designer or Specialty Contractor, by a third party, or a combination. A third-party firm may not be qualified for certain specialized tasks in the chapter; then the geotechnical engineer or wall designer must complete them. The Owner or wall designer establishes who inspects what. Porterfield et al. (1994) give more detail on methods, nail testing, forms and difficult ground. 9.3.2 Excavation (pp. 234-235): (1) mass excavation for equipment access and site grading; (2) bench excavations to the finished wall line ('neat line'). During mass excavation verify it does not encroach on the partially completed wall; the Contractor completes the excavation to neat line and grade, verified within tolerance. Report or note: type, nature and moisture of excavated and face materials (moisture and seepage, soft zones, sloughing and overbreaks, boulders, manmade features, with sketches); unexpected soft zones, seepage areas or fill, reported to the designer (seepage may need added drainage; soft soil or fill not considered in design may warrant a design revision); recurrent raveling or sloughing (report to the Owner; the Contractor addresses overbreaks and protruding cobbles or boulders); condition of the face at the start and end of each day and unprotected portions (generally not left unprotected overnight); and the stability of the retained soils, the area behind or upslope and the excavation bottom, at least twice a day, examining the ground surface for cracks and seepage and noting utilities, manholes and pavements, with conditions recorded on the first day. Ground movements may occur behind the wall to a distance equal to the wall height; inspection beyond is usually unnecessary.
key_points: Inspectors: Geotechnical Engineer, wall Designer or Specialty Contractor, third party, or a combination
Specialized tasks a third party is not qualified for go to the geotechnical engineer or wall designer
Mass excavation must not encroach on the partially completed wall
Bench excavation to the neat line and grade within the specified tolerance
Unexpected soft zones, seepage or fill reported to the designer; may warrant design revision
Face generally not left unprotected overnight; stability checked at least twice a day
Ground movements may extend behind the wall a distance equal to the wall height
sections.applicability: Organization of construction inspection and inspection of soil nail wall excavation.

sections.title: Drilling
sections.summary: Drill holes are located and oriented as on the plans within tolerance; deviations are reported to the Owner. Mast angle, measured with an angle tool, must represent the tendon inclination at the face. The inspector records the equipment and method, drill fluid (or HBSN grout) pressure, flow and volume, return flush problems, ground subsidence, drilling tools and lengths, final hole length and bit diameter, and how long the hole stays open; for hollow bars, drilling rate, grout pressure, bit and grout ports, and cuttings.
sections.body: 9.3.3 Drilling (pp. 235-237). Holes located and oriented as on the plans within the specified tolerances; deviations noted and communicated to the Owner. The drill mast angle is generally measured with an angle tool placed on the mast, taking care that it represents the tendon inclination as it enters the face. Report or note: the equipment and installation method (Chapter 3); the pressure, flow rate and volume of drill fluid (or grout for HBSNs), noting whether return flush clogs, connects with other holes or the ground surface, or causes heaving; subsidence of ground above the drilling or large soil removal with little advance (the Contractor must modify procedures); the drilling method and tools (bit type, casing diameter and final length, drill string length, drilling fluid type), cuttings, fluid loss, zones of difficult and easy drilling, and effective drilling time as a site-specific indicator; the lengths of bit, drill string and casing sections before drilling, the final hole length after flushing and before tendon insertion, and the bit diameter (equivalent to the nominal hole diameter); and the time the hole is left open (holes in soil kept open only briefly; generally insert and grout the tendon immediately after drilling, exceptions set project by project with flushing as needed). Hollow bar installation: record the drilling rate and grout pressure (cuttings are hard to see when grout is the drilling fluid; note consistent grout return to the face), the drill bit type and number and size of grout exit ports, and the type of soil cuttings (occasionally sieve-wash the outflow grout, useful in widely graded or organic soils).
key_points: Location and orientation within specified tolerances; deviations communicated to the Owner
Mast angle by angle tool must represent the tendon inclination entering the face
Record drill fluid (or HBSN grout) pressure, flow rate and volume; watch return flush, connections, heave
Subsidence or large soil removal without advance: Contractor modifies drilling procedures
Record drilling tools and lengths, final hole length, bit diameter (= nominal hole diameter)
Holes in soil open only briefly; tendon generally inserted and grouted immediately after drilling
HBSN: record drilling rate, grout pressure, bit and grout ports, soil cuttings
sections.applicability: Inspection of soil nail drilling, including hollow bar soil nails.

sections.title: Tendon Installation and Grouting
sections.summary: Each tendon is checked for length, diameter, grade, centralizers and corrosion protection and inserted to the minimum length; failure to insert indicates caving or sloughing. Grout is tremied from the hole bottom in one continuous process, tremie end below the grout surface. Grout volume should be at least the theoretical hole volume, often 10 to 30 percent more; below 100 or above 130 percent, the Contractor and Owner are notified. Fluid grout specific gravity (typically 1.8 to 1.9) is the primary QC check, preferred to cube tests.
sections.body: 9.3.4 Tendon Installation (p. 237): verify each tendon meets the length, diameter, steel grade, centralizer and corrosion protection requirements; insert to the minimum specified length; inability to do so indicates an unacceptable condition from caving or sloughing (insufficient drilled length can be ruled out from the inspector's drilling log). Handle tendons carefully with adequate support when lifted; centralizers stiff and large enough for the minimum grout cover, spaced per drawings or specifications, not impeding tremied grout or, for HBSNs, drilling grout and cuttings. 9.3.5 Grouting (pp. 237-239): the full nail length should be grouted without voids, soil intrusion or gaps; not directly verifiable, so checked indirectly by inspecting the hole before grouting and recording the grout volume. Grout by tremie pipe inserted to the hole bottom in a continuous process; if withdrawn as grouting proceeds, the end stays below the grout surface. Grouting may precede or follow tendon insertion (if after, the tendon volume enters the theoretical volume; the tremie hose is attached so it does not coil and can be pulled without damage), or be done in a temporary casing. With hollow-stem augers, the auger rotation must not be reversed during extraction (soil mixes into the grout, reducing bond). Grout volume is measured by a calibrated tank or flowmeter from when final grout enters to when it exits free of impurities; it must be at least the theoretical volume, often 10 to 30 percent larger; below 100 or above 130 percent, the Contractor and Owner are notified and remedial measures taken if needed. Specific gravity of newly prepared fluid grout should be the primary QC for production nails, preferred to compression tests, as it tracks water-cement ratio and so strength. Cubes of known specific gravity made with project equipment are tested at the start for each mix; if they meet the specified strength, that specific gravity becomes the QC tool, with further comparison cubes for long projects or changes in cement, water, admixtures, batching or mixing. Specific gravity is measured with an API balance (Baroid mud balance) per ASTM D4380 or API RP 13B; target typically 1.8 to 1.9 for pumpable grout above the commonly used 4,000 psi; cubes tested per ASTM C109; specifications set test type and minimum frequency. HBSN drilling grout may be 1.4 to 1.6; a heavier final grout (1.8 to 1.9) is pumped through the bar and the nail is complete when it returns to the face.
key_points: Verify tendon length, diameter, grade, centralizers and corrosion protection; insert to minimum length
Inability to insert indicates caving or sloughing (drilled length checked from the drilling log)
Tremie from the hole bottom, continuous; tremie end kept below the grout surface
Hollow-stem auger: no reverse rotation during extraction
Grout volume at least theoretical, often 10-30% more; <100% or >130%: notify Contractor and Owner
Fluid grout specific gravity is the primary QC (target typically 1.8-1.9), preferred to cube tests
Specific gravity by mud balance (ASTM D4380 / API RP 13B); cubes per ASTM C109
HBSN: drilling grout 1.4-1.6; final grout 1.8-1.9 pumped until it returns to the face
sections.applicability: Inspection of tendon installation and grouting, including grout volume and specific gravity QC.

sections.title: Geocomposite Strip Drains and Wall Facing
sections.summary: Strip drains are placed vertically at specified intervals, continuous top to bottom, with any impermeable liner facing the shotcrete, not the soil; at the base they connect to a footing drain or to weep holes. Footing drain pipes are not wrapped in filter fabric. Shotcrete quality depends most on an experienced nozzleman (ACI or ASA certification and a test panel may be required). Nozzle perpendicular to the surface, 2 to 5 ft for wet-mix and 3 to 6 ft for dry-mix, starting at the bottom; bearing plates set in wet shotcrete without voids.
sections.body: 9.3.6 Geocomposite Strip Drains (p. 239): after each lift's final excavation and nail installation, drains are placed vertically at specified intervals, continuous from top to bottom, per drawings and specifications; an impermeable protective liner on one side must not contact the soil but be positioned to receive shotcrete. At the base, drains connect either to a footing drain below finished grade or to weep holes through the finished wall, located as on the plans at the drain locations, with filter fabric behind the weep holes (or fabric-wrapped drainage aggregate). Footing drains are perforated pipe in drainage gravel, sloped as on the plans; the pipe is not wrapped in filter fabric, though the aggregate may be. 9.3.7 Wall Facing (pp. 239-241): reinforcing steel then shotcrete to the lines and grades; WWM and bars at the proper dimensions, locations and overlap. Shotcrete facing may be placed before nails where standup time is poor or by Contractor preference. Conventional shotcrete procedures apply (Appendices E and F); avoid equipment causing excessive vibration nearby (rebound); clean the overlying cold joint before the underlying lift (water and air, or air), without eroding the cut below. The most critical factor is an experienced nozzleman; specifications may require ACI or American Shotcrete Association certification and a pre-qualification test panel. Practices: nozzle perpendicular to the surface except around bars; optimum nozzle distance 2 to 5 ft wet-mix, 3 to 6 ft dry-mix; start at the bottom; no voids behind bars, plates or mesh; screen boards, guide wires or depth spacers for sharp edges and lines. The inspector checks lines, minimum thickness within tolerance, finish and inclination, bearing plates with headed studs set while the shotcrete is wet without voids (proper number and diameter of studs for initial facing), and for cast-in-place final facing, the usual concrete inspection (reinforcement placement, thicknesses, no deleterious material).
key_points: Strip drains vertical at specified intervals, continuous top to bottom
Impermeable liner positioned to receive shotcrete, not in contact with the soil
Base connection to a footing drain or to weep holes; perforated footing pipe not wrapped in filter fabric
Shotcrete may precede nail installation where standup time is poor
Clean the overlying cold joint before shooting the underlying lift
Experienced nozzleman most critical; ACI or ASA certification and test panel may be required
Nozzle perpendicular; 2-5 ft wet-mix, 3-6 ft dry-mix; start at the bottom; no voids behind steel
Bearing plates with headed studs set while the shotcrete is wet, without voids underneath
sections.applicability: Inspection of strip drains, shotcrete facing and cast-in-place final facing.

sections.title: Load Testing
sections.summary: Load tests verify that nail design loads are carried without excessive movement and with an adequate factor of safety, and check the Contractor's drilling, installation and grouting. Testing in each row is normally completed before the next lower level (the Engineer may relax this). Verification tests on sacrificial nails check design bond values, commonly two per major stratum; proof tests on at least 5 percent of production nails check uniformity; creep tests, part of both, hold a constant load for 10 to 60 minutes.
sections.body: 9.4.1 Introduction (pp. 241-243). Testing verifies that design loads are carried without excessive movement and with an adequate factor of safety, and the adequacy of drilling, installation and grouting before and during construction; changed ground or procedures may need more testing. Standard practice completes testing in each row before the next lower level, which the Engineer may relax, most often for long walls. Faulty practices or low resistance require the Contractor to alter methods; test procedures and acceptance criteria belong in the specifications. The inspector observes and logs the tests and may help select proof test nails. Test nails need a bonded length in the layer of interest and an unbonded length above (in proof tests, the minimum stressing length), by any effective debonding method; grout must not be pumped above the bond length (load transfer through grout in the unbonded zone, the 'donut' effect of Cadden et al. 2010, gives artificially high bond). A painted centralizer or survey ribbon can mark the top of the bond zone; after acceptance the unbonded length is grouted. For HBSNs, creating an unbonded length is difficult (flushing grout with a tremie and water, or a smooth-casing bond breaker, which gave artificially high bond per Cadden et al.); no accepted procedure exists, so reported HBSN bond strengths vary greatly. 9.4.1a Verification tests check the Contractor's pullout capacity against design values, to a load inducing at least the nominal design bond (an oversized tendon may be needed to reach pullout); their number is set by the Engineer, commonly two per major stratum, or by design nail length; on sacrificial nails. 9.4.1b Proof tests on at least 5 percent of production nails, chosen using installation records (irregular drilling, low grout take, redrilled nails nearby); verification tests do not count toward the 5 percent. 9.4.1c Creep tests, part of verification and proof tests, hold a constant load for 10 to 60 minutes.
key_points: Testing in each row completed before the next lower level; the Engineer may relax this
Test nails: bonded length in the stratum of interest and an unbonded length above
Grout above the bond length gives artificially high bond (the 'donut' effect)
HBSN: no accepted method for an unbonded zone; reported bond strengths vary greatly
Verification tests: sacrificial nails, at least the nominal design bond; commonly two per major stratum
Proof tests: at least 5% of production nails, chosen from installation records; verification tests excluded
Creep tests: constant load held 10 to 60 minutes, part of verification and proof tests
sections.applicability: Purpose, types and selection of soil nail load tests.

sections.title: Equipment for Testing and Details of Verification Testing
sections.summary: A center-hole jack, aligned with the nail, reacts on a frame or block, not the grout column; alignment load at most 2.5 percent of the maximum test load; test load at most 80 percent of jack capacity. One or two dial gauges read to 0.001 in. Verification nails have an unbonded length at least 3 ft inside the hole and a bonded length LB VT of at least 10 ft, below LB VT max (Eqs 9.1, 9.2). VTL = LB VT x rPO (Eq 9.3) is an ultimate load. Table 9.1 holds 0.75 VTL 60 min for creep. Acceptance: no pullout below VTL; movement > 0.8 of elastic elongation (Eq 9.4).
sections.body: 9.4.2 Equipment for Testing (pp. 243-245): center-hole hydraulic jack and pump, jack axis aligned with the nail; a jacking frame or reaction block between face and jack, sized not to overstress the shotcrete or bearing surface, not reacting on the grout column. Alignment load (AL) not over 2.5 percent of the maximum test load; jack sized so the test load is not over 80 percent of its rated capacity (Figures 9.1, 9.2). Nail head movement by at least one, preferably two, dial gauges on an independent support, within 5 degrees of the nail axis, zeroed after AL, reading to 0.001 in., with travel at least the estimated elastic elongation plus 1 in., or at least 2 in. A pressure gauge correlates jack load; a center-hole load cell may be added for creep tests (pressure gauges lack resolution over long holds); recent calibrations obtained before testing (Figure 9.3). 9.4.3 Details of Verification Testing (pp. 246-250): on sacrificial nails before construction, and during production for new conditions or methods, built as production nails; ideally to pullout. They give the actual bond resistance (if taken to pullout), confirm it exceeds the nominal design value, and show creep potential; loads above the nominal bond, preferably to pullout, are desirable. Fully grouted nails must not be used; the unbonded length runs from the bearing plate to the bond zone and is at least 3 ft within the hole, plus jack and tail length outside. LB VT is chosen so the bond limit is reached first: (1) LB VT max from Eq 9.1 (Grades 60 and 75, ASTM A615) or Eq 9.2 (Grade 150, ASTM A722); (2) if over 10 ft, choose 10 ft <= LB VT <= LB VT max; (3) if under 10 ft, set LB VT = 10 ft and enlarge the tendon until LB VT max > 10 ft. VTL (Eq 9.3) is an ultimate load, not a design load as in the previous manual, so the Table 9.1 factors differ; it carries no pullout safety or resistance factor. Loads above VTL are optional; unload/reload cycles are rare. Table 9.1: each increment held at least 10 minutes, creep test at 0.75 VTL; optional stepped unloading (one to seven steps). Acceptance: no pullout below 1.00 VTL; total movement at VTL over 80 percent of the theoretical elastic elongation of the unbonded length (Eq 9.4), so load transfers only in the bonded length; creep per Section 9.4.5. Figures 9.4 and 9.5: data sheet and data reduction.
key_points: Alignment load <= 2.5% of maximum test load; test load <= 80% of rated jack capacity
Dial gauges within 5 degrees of the nail axis, 0.001 in., travel elastic elongation + 1 in. or at least 2 in.
Unbonded length at least 3 ft within the drill hole; fully grouted test nails not used
Eq 9.1: LB VT max = At fy CRTY / rPO (CRTY = 0.9); Eq 9.2: At fu CRTU / rPO (CRTU = 0.8)
LB VT at least 10 ft and not over LB VT max; enlarge the tendon if LB VT max < 10 ft
Eq 9.3: VTL = LB VT x rPO, an ultimate load with no safety or resistance factor
Table 9.1: 0.13 to 1.00 VTL in 10-min holds; 0.75 VTL held 60 min as the creep test
Acceptance: no pullout below 1.00 VTL; Eq 9.4 movement > 0.8 VTL LUB / (E At); creep per 9.4.5

sections.title: Details of Proof Tests, Details of Creep Tests, and Strain Gauges
sections.summary: Proof test nails have an unbonded length at least 3 ft inside the hole and a bonded length of 10 ft or LB PT max (Eqs 9.5, 9.6, with rPO x 0.75 below the line), whichever is smaller. PTL = LB PT x rPO x 0.75 (Eq 9.7). Creep test at 1.00 PTL. Acceptance: no pullout below PTL; movement > 0.8 PTL LUB/(E At) (Eq 9.8). Creep: < 0.04 in. between 1 and 10 min (0.75 VTL or PTL); < 0.08 in. between 6 and 60 min; verification creep rate linear or decreasing. Strain gauges give load along the nail.
sections.body: 9.4.4 Details of Proof Tests (pp. 253-255): single-cycle tests to a maximum proof test load (PTL). The temporary unbonded length runs from the bearing plate to the grouted length and is at least 3 ft within the hole, plus jack and tail length. LB PT is chosen so the bond limit comes first: (1) LB PT max from Eq 9.5 (text: Grade 75 and other A615 mild steel; caption: Grades 60 and 75) or Eq 9.6 (Grade 150, A722); (2) LB PT = 10 ft or LB PT max, whichever is smaller. Production proof nails shorter than 12 ft may be tested with less than 10 ft of bond; fully grouted nails must not be proof tested. PTL by Eq 9.7, a maximum load, so the Table 9.2 schedule differs from the previous manual. The text says each increment is held at least 10 minutes; Table 9.2 as printed holds 0.17 to 0.83 PTL 'until movement stabilizes' (10 minutes with readings at 1, 2, 5, 10 recommended in creep-susceptible soils). Creep test at 1.00 PTL. Acceptance: no pullout below 1.0 PTL; total movement at PTL over 80 percent of the theoretical elastic elongation (Eq 9.8); creep per Section 9.4.5. 9.4.5 Details of Creep Tests (pp. 255-256): deflection versus log-time on a semi-log plot. Verification tests: creep between 1 and 10 minutes at 0.75 VTL under 0.04 in.; between 6 and 60 minutes under 0.08 in.; creep rate linear or decreasing. Proof tests: under 0.04 in. between 1 and 10 minutes; if exceeded, hold PTL 50 more minutes (readings at 20, 30, 50, 60) and require under 0.08 in. between 6 and 60 minutes. The criteria come from ground anchor experience (Figure 9.6). 9.4.6 Strain Gauges (pp. 257-258): tendon strain with steel modulus (typically 29,000 ksi) gives axial load; several spot-weldable gauges give the load distribution and average mobilized bond between gauges, and when bond is fully mobilized along part of the nail. Ignoring the grout's stiffness (assumed cracked) can overestimate mobilized bond at low loads; include the grout modulus when strain is below its tensile limit strain. Gauges give actual bond where pullout does not occur and bond in each of several strata; use redundant gauges where critical.
key_points: Proof test unbonded length at least 3 ft within the drill hole; fully grouted nails not proof tested
Eq 9.5/9.6: LB PT max = At fy CRTY / (rPO x 0.75) or At fu CRTU / (rPO x 0.75)
LB PT = 10 ft or LB PT max, whichever is smaller; nails under 12 ft may have less than 10 ft of bond
Eq 9.7: PTL = LB PT x rPO x 0.75
Table 9.2: 0.17 to 0.83 PTL until movement stabilizes; 1.0 PTL creep test 10 min
Acceptance: no pullout below 1.0 PTL; Eq 9.8 movement > 0.8 PTL LUB / (E At)
Creep: < 0.04 in. 1-10 min; < 0.08 in. 6-60 min; proof test extended 50 min if 0.04 in. exceeded
Verification creep rate must be linear or decreasing
Strain gauges: load distribution and mobilized bond; account for grout modulus at low strain

If movement between 1 and 10 min exceeds 0.04 in., hold PTL 50 more minutes (readings at 20, 30, 50, 60). In creep-susceptible soils hold each increment 10 min (readings at 1, 2, 5, 10).

sections.title: Instrumentation and Monitoring
sections.summary: Performance monitoring should be included for critical or unusual walls (road widening under existing bridges, high surcharge) and considered for an Owner's first permanent wall; at least 1 year of post-construction monitoring is recommended. A minimum plan measures face movement (survey markers and inclinometers 3 to 8 ft behind the facing, not beyond 30 percent of wall height for one row), top-of-wall and ground movements, ground cracks, facing deterioration and drainage. The plan sets instruments, reading and reporting frequency; threshold criteria and an action plan are essential.
sections.body: 9.5.1 Introduction (p. 258): monitoring should be included in critical or unusual installations (road widening under existing bridges, high surcharge) and considered when an Owner builds its first permanent soil nail wall; instruments include inclinometers, top-of-wall survey points, load cells and strain gauges; monitoring for at least 1 year after construction is recommended to examine service deformation and stresses with load, time and environment (e.g., freeze-thaw). 9.5.2 Monitored Parameters (pp. 258-259): deformation of the wall or slope is the most significant indicator; inclinometers give the most comprehensive data; survey points at the top and on the face correlate with them. 9.5.3 Monitoring and Action Plan (pp. 259-261): at a minimum, horizontal face movement (surface markers by optical survey; inclinometer casings 3 to 8 ft behind the facing, generally not farther than 30 percent of the wall height for one row); vertical and horizontal movement of the top of facing and ground behind; ground cracks behind the wall (daily visual inspection, crack gauges if needed); local movement or deterioration of the facing; drainage behavior (outflow points or standpipe piezometers). More comprehensive plans may monitor the toe in fine-grained soils (basal heave or global instability), moving ground, design changes or value engineering, excavation rates, or research; they may add strain gauges in diametrically opposed pairs at 5-ft spacing and inclinometer arrays (Figure 9.7). The plan defines instrument type and location, measurement, observation and reporting frequency, minimum reporting requirements and reporting lines. Movement threshold criteria and an action plan are essential; the action plan is typically developed by the Contractor, with minimum actions possibly in the specifications. 9.5.4 Monitoring Instruments (pp. 261-263): selected for the parameter, reliability, simplicity and readout compatibility. Inclinometers: in-place units give rapid full-depth readings but should be checked periodically with a manual probe. Survey points: reflector prisms read optically or by EDM, typically 0.1 in. or better within 300 ft; automated total stations reduce reading errors, separate environmental from gravity-induced movement and may save cost on long projects. Strain gauges: vibrating wire gauges on sister bars most common in the U.S. (Figure 9.8); spot-weldable vibrating wire, optical fiber and resistance gauges also used. Load cells at the nail head (Wheatstone-resistance bridges, or vibrating wire) give facing loads over time but occasionally read inaccurately.
key_points: Monitoring for critical or unusual walls; considered for an Owner's first permanent soil nail wall
At least 1 year of post-construction monitoring recommended
Inclinometers 3-8 ft behind the facing, generally not beyond 30% of wall height for a single row
Minimum plan: face, top-of-wall and ground movements, ground cracks, facing deterioration, drainage
Threshold criteria and an action plan are essential; action plan typically by the Contractor
Strain gauges in diametrically opposed pairs at 5-ft spacing in comprehensive plans
Survey points 0.1 in. or better within 300 ft; automated total stations reduce reading errors
Nail head load cells occasionally read inaccurately; interpret with care
